note: Synthetic, hand-written, no private data. Shaped like the Phase 1 corpus: every turn a memo, the house tics, everyone talking to the chair, no questions, no interruptions. Used by the metrics self-test to check that the realism index ranks it below realism-target.json.

events.title: Sunday opening
events.motion: The bakery should open on Sundays.

events.speaker: marcus
events.text: I want the case for first and I want it with numbers. Ana, you go first. Bo, you answer her directly. Cy, you weigh the two openings from your own discipline and tell me which one is closer to right. I am putting it to you in writing: no motion closes on assertion in this room.

events.speaker: ana
events.text:
Marcus, the case for Sunday is not a revenue question, it is a utilisation question. The ovens sit cold for a full day while rent, insurance and the lease clock keep running, and that idle day is the single largest unpriced cost in the business (observed, from eleven years running bakeries on two high streets). A Sunday trade does not need to match Saturday to pay for itself; it needs to clear the incremental wage bill and the extra flour, and on the footfall I have seen that is a low bar.

I will own my bias out loud: I hate idle ovens, and I have argued this in every shop I have ever run. But the arithmetic does not care about my bias. If the room wants a falsifier, mine is simple: if a four-week trial cannot cover its own wages by week three, I withdraw the motion. Until then, the burden sits with whoever wants the ovens cold, and Marcus, I would ask the desk to pull last year's Saturday takings so we can anchor the Sunday estimate.

events.speaker: bo
events.text:
Ana is closer to right on the cost side, and her own proposal is why it fails. The binding constraint here is not utilisation, it is labour. Two of the four staff already work six days, and a seventh day is not an extra shift, it is a resignation risk (observed, from nine years of studying staffing in shops this size). The strongest version of Ana's case assumes the rota stretches, and in a four-person shop it does not stretch, it snaps.

Let me name the cost plainly. If one of the two six-day bakers leaves, the replacement takes six to ten weeks to hire and train, and every one of those weeks the Saturday trade, which is the real profit day, runs short. So the honest comparison is not Sunday revenue against Sunday wages; it is Sunday revenue against the expected cost of losing a baker. Marcus, I would want the desk to price that before anyone rules on this.

events.speaker: cy
events.text:
What everyone is missing is that footfall on this street is not evenly spread across the weekend, it is front-loaded into Saturday morning. Sunday trade on comparable high streets runs at roughly sixty percent of Saturday, and most of that sixty percent arrives between ten and one (observed, from footfall counters on six comparable streets). So both openings are arguing about a full Sunday when the real choice is a short Sunday.

Bo is closer to right on the labour risk, and Ana is closer to right on the idle cost, and the short Sunday is the version where both of their claims survive. A ten-to-two opening needs one baker for the early bake and one person on the counter, which is a rota that does not touch the two six-day staff at all. I will say it against my own book: I usually argue for the full day. Marcus, the decision rule I would put to the room is that the trial runs short and expands only on evidence.

events.speaker: marcus
events.text: I want the short Sunday attacked rather than admired. Bo, you go first: does a ten-to-two rota really leave the six-day staff untouched? Ana, then you. Cy, hold your fire until both have answered. I am putting it to you in writing that nobody concedes without naming what moved them.

events.speaker: bo
events.text:
Concession first, Marcus, because Cy earned it: the short Sunday is not the version I was attacking, it is a different motion, and on that motion my resignation argument mostly falls away. A ten-to-two shift staffed by the two people who do not already work six days is a rota that holds, and I withdraw the claim that any Sunday snaps the rota (observed, from the shift patterns I have studied in shops of this size).

But the concession is narrow and I will name its cost. The early bake starts at five, not ten, so the baker on that shift works a nine-hour day even on a short opening, and the two staff without six-day weeks are the counter staff, not the bakers. So the question that is still open is who bakes at five on Sunday. Until the room answers that, my falsifier has not fired, and I would ask Marcus to put it to the founder directly.

events.speaker: ana
events.text:
Bo is closer to right on the five o'clock bake, and that is the whole problem with my original case, not a footnote to it. The idle oven is not a cost the short Sunday removes, it is a cost the short Sunday moves to five in the morning, and somebody has to be in the building to pay it. I will take the correction: my utilisation argument assumed the bake was free, and it is not.

The route nobody has priced is the Saturday overbake. If Saturday's late bake runs one extra batch of the long-life lines, the sourdough and the rye, they hold for a Sunday counter without a baker in the building at all, and the short Sunday becomes a counter shift only (observed, from two shops that ran exactly this pattern). So the answer is to price the Saturday overbake against a Sunday baker's wage, and Marcus, that is a number the desk can produce from last year's waste figures.

events.speaker: cy
events.text:
The Saturday overbake is not a workaround, it is the design, and it changes what the trial measures. If Sunday sells only long-life lines, the trial is no longer asking whether Sunday trade covers a baker; it is asking whether Sunday customers will buy yesterday's bread at full price, which is a demand question my footfall numbers cannot answer (assumed, from what I know of comparable streets).

So I will say it plainly: the motion the room can actually rule on is a four-week, counter-only, ten-to-two Sunday selling the Saturday overbake, with a kill rule at week three. That keeps Bo's six-day staff untouched, prices Ana's idle-oven cost honestly, and turns my footfall estimate into something the trial measures instead of something we argue about. Marcus, that is the ruling I would put to the room.

decision.decision: Run a four-week, counter-only, ten-to-two Sunday trial selling the Saturday overbake, with a kill rule at week three.
decision.rationale: The short Sunday keeps the six-day staff off the rota and turns the footfall estimate into a measurement.

dissents.position: No Sunday without a named five o'clock baker.
dissents.reasoning: The overbake moves the early shift to Saturday night.
